subChunks.title: The Genealogical Proof Standard
subChunks.hookHtml: A name on a document is not proof of an ancestor. The Board for Certification of Genealogists publishes a five-element standard that separates a guess from a finding — and it is the difference between a hobbyist's tree and one a professional will sign their name to.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What the GPS is, and why it exists

The Genealogical Proof Standard (GPS) is the framework the Board for Certification of Genealogists (BCG) uses to evaluate whether a conclusion about identity, relationship, or event is credible. It is published in the BCG's Genealogy Standards (2nd ed., 2019). It exists because genealogy works almost exclusively from incomplete, ambiguous, sometimes contradictory records — and yet it produces conclusions that families, courts, and lineage societies act upon. Without a shared standard, every researcher's tree is just a private opinion.

The five elements

A conclusion meets the standard only when all five elements have been satisfied. Skipping any one of them — and especially skipping the first — collapses the argument.

#ElementWhat it asks of you
1Reasonably exhaustive searchYou have searched every record set a competent researcher would consult for this question, in this place, at this time.
2Complete, accurate source citationsEvery claim is backed by a citation specific enough that another researcher can find the same source and read the same words.
3Skilled analysis and correlation of the evidenceYou have weighed each piece of evidence on its own — original vs derivative, primary vs secondary, direct vs indirect — and put the pieces together.
4Resolution of conflicting evidenceWhere records disagree, you have explained why and shown which conclusion the weight of evidence supports.
5Soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusionYour finding is presented as a written argument — a proof statement, summary, or argument — that another researcher can follow and challenge.

Why "I found a match" is not proof

A common mistake: searching one database (say, FamilySearch's 1850 U.S. Census), finding one entry that fits the name and approximate age, and adding the person to a tree. This satisfies none of the five elements. It is one record from one source, with no analysis of whether other people of that name lived in the area, no consideration that ages on the census are routinely off by years, no citation a stranger could follow without rummaging through your notes, and no written argument explaining why this John Walker is your John Walker rather than the other three living in the same county.

Worked example — a 19th-century identity claim

Suppose your research question is: Was the John Walker who married Mary Ellis in Lancashire in 1849 the same John Walker who appeared as a labourer in the 1851 census of Preston?

  • Element 1 — exhaustive search. You consult: the parish marriage register, the 1851 census, the 1841 census (to see who else of that name was in the county), parish baptism records for any children, possible burial records, newspaper notices, and the General Register Office indexes for England & Wales. You record what you searched and what came up empty.
  • Element 2 — citations. Each record gets a full citation: parish, register, page, entry number, repository, and database access details if used online (see gen-b2).
  • Element 3 — analysis. You note that the 1849 marriage names a wife "Mary" and the 1851 census shows a wife "Mary" of approximately the right age in the same town. You also note that "John Walker" was the third-most-common male name in Lancashire — so name-and-place is weak on its own.
  • Element 4 — conflict resolution. The marriage register gives John's age as 24; the 1851 census gives 28 (a four-year gap in two years). You note that ages on 19th-century English censuses are often rounded or self-reported and treat the discrepancy as plausible rather than disqualifying — but you say so explicitly.
  • Element 5 — written conclusion. You write a paragraph that concludes: "The weight of evidence — shared first name, matching wife's first name, identical parish of residence, plausible age progression, and absence of any other John-and-Mary Walker couple of the right age in the 1851 Preston census — supports the conclusion that the 1849 marriage record and the 1851 census refer to the same couple."

    That is a defensible finding. It may still be wrong — genealogy rarely produces certainty — but it has been argued, and another researcher can either accept it or attack it on its weakest point.

    How a claim fails

    The same question fails the GPS if you stopped at the marriage register and the census, found one of each, and called it done. The argument has nothing to push back against — and the moment a second John Walker turns up in Preston, your tree is wrong and you have no record of why you ever believed otherwise.

storyBeats.text: Theodora of the Thousand Names is bent over an oak desk, a stack of grey card-bound notebooks open in front of her. She does not look up as you sit down — she finishes the line she is writing, blots it, then closes the notebook with deliberate care.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: There is a moment — every genealogist has it — when you find a name that fits. The town is right. The age is roughly right. The wife's name even matches. And in that moment you want to write the line into your tree and move on. Don't. Don't. That is the moment professionals are trained to slow down.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: The Board for Certification of Genealogists publishes a standard. Five elements. Reasonably exhaustive search; complete and accurate citations; skilled analysis and correlation; resolution of conflicts; a soundly reasoned written conclusion. All five. A conclusion that satisfies four out of five is not 80 percent right — it is undefended.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: I have seen apprentices spend six months on one ancestor and produce three lines of proof. That is correct. I have seen others build trees ten generations deep in an afternoon and produce nothing of value. The GPS is what tells the difference between depth and speed.

storyBeats.speaker: The five elements — memorise them
storyBeats.text:
1. Reasonably exhaustive search
2. Complete, accurate source citations
3. Skilled analysis and correlation of the evidence
4. Resolution of conflicting evidence
5. Soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Each of the next four lessons covers one element more deeply — citation, exhaustive search, conflict resolution, the research log. Hold them all in your head at once. They are not a checklist to tick; they are five lenses you turn on the same problem until it has no shadows left.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Study prompt

Pick one ancestor in your own (or a sample) family tree whose identity you have asserted. For that single person, walk through the five elements honestly:

  1. What records did I actually search? What records would a competent researcher have searched that I didn't?
  2. Could a stranger find each source from my citation alone, without help from me?
  3. Did I weigh each record's reliability, or did I treat a transcription on Ancestry the same as the original parish register?
  4. Where records disagreed, did I pick the one I liked — or did I write down why I chose one over the other?
  5. Have I ever written my conclusion as a paragraph another researcher could attack?

Most apprentices fail at least three of the five on their first honest pass. That is normal. The point of the standard is not to make you feel inadequate — it is to show you what "finished" actually looks like.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a thoughtful relative who has just bought their first DNA test why "I found a match in the 1850 census" is not the same as proving an ancestor. Use the five elements of the GPS to structure your explanation.

questions.questionHtml: The Genealogical Proof Standard, as published by the Board for Certification of Genealogists, has how many elements?
options: Five
Three
Seven
Ten
questions.correctAnswer: Five
questions.explanationHtml: Five: reasonably exhaustive search; complete and accurate source citations; skilled analysis and correlation; resolution of conflicting evidence; soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion. Memorise them — they are the spine of every credible genealogical argument.

questions.questionHtml: Which of these is not one of the five elements of the GPS?
options: DNA confirmation of every conclusion
Reasonably exhaustive search
Resolution of conflicting evidence
Soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion
questions.correctAnswer: DNA confirmation of every conclusion
questions.explanationHtml: DNA evidence is one type of evidence the standard can accommodate, but it is not itself an element of the GPS. The standard predates widespread genetic genealogy and applies to documentary research where DNA is unavailable (e.g. anyone born before about 1840 in most regions).

questions.questionHtml: An apprentice claims her great-great-grandfather was Thomas Reilly, born in Galway in 1834. Her evidence: she found one entry on FamilySearch labelled "Thomas Reilly, Galway, 1834" and added him to her tree. Which GPS element has she most clearly failed?
options: Reasonably exhaustive search — she has consulted exactly one record set
Element 5 — she has written a beautiful conclusion but with no evidence
Element 4 — she has unresolved conflicting evidence
She has met the standard; further research would be over-engineering
questions.correctAnswer: Reasonably exhaustive search — she has consulted exactly one record set
questions.explanationHtml: One database is the opposite of exhaustive. Without checking civil registration, parish baptisms, the 1841/1851 censuses, neighbouring parishes (Reilly is one of the most common Galway surnames), and at least the FamilySearch image of the original (rather than a transcribed index entry), the conclusion has nothing supporting it. She has also failed elements 2, 3, and 5 — but element 1 is the headline failure.

questions.questionHtml: Two researchers analyse the same question. Whose work meets the GPS?
options: Researcher A consulted six record types, cited each one, weighed contradictions explicitly, and wrote a one-page argument concluding which John Walker is the ancestor
Researcher B found three records that agreed, copied them into her notes, and added the person to her tree without writing further
Researcher C found one DNA match at the third-cousin level and added an entire branch from that match's published tree
Researcher D consulted twenty record types but kept all the analysis in her head and wrote no conclusion
questions.correctAnswer: Researcher A consulted six record types, cited each one, weighed contradictions explicitly, and wrote a one-page argument concluding which John Walker is the ancestor
questions.explanationHtml: Only A meets all five elements. B fails on exhaustive search, analysis, and the written conclusion. C imports an unverified tree from a stranger — the worst kind of failure. D may have done excellent thinking but has not produced a written argument others can engage with, and unwritten reasoning cannot be checked, defended, or built upon.

subChunks.title: Source Citation — the Evidence Explained Model
subChunks.hookHtml: An academic citation tells you which book to find. A genealogical citation tells you which image in which database, originally drawn from which register, held in which archive, accessed on which date. Five layers, not one. Elizabeth Shown Mills wrote the manual.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why genealogy citations are deeper

Academic citation answers a single question: where did this idea come from? Genealogy citation has to answer five:

LayerWhat it identifies
1. The source itselfThe actual record — "1851 census of England and Wales, Lancashire, Preston, ED 7, p. 14"
2. The repositoryWhere the original is held — "The National Archives, Kew, RG 11/4012"
3. The intermediary (if any)The film, microfilm, or database that carries the image — "FamilySearch, image group 005009123"
4. The format / specific access pathURL or shelfmark — "https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HT-XJ4Q-Y"
5. The access dateWhen you saw it — "accessed 7 May 2026"

This depth exists because genealogical sources move. A parish register is reorganised; a database URL changes; a microfilm is digitised; a transcript is corrected. A citation that names only the parish register without the access date and intermediary may be unreproducible in five years.

The Evidence Explained framework

Elizabeth Shown Mills, Evidence Explained: Citing History Sources from Artifacts to Cyberspace (4th ed., Genealogical Publishing Co., 2024), is the standard reference. It is dense — over 800 pages — but its core idea is simple:

  • Cite the layer of the source you actually used. If you read a database transcript, cite the transcript and the database. If you read a microfilm of the original register, cite the register, the archive, and the film. If you read the original document at the archive, cite the document and the archive.
  • Cite the layers behind it that produced what you saw. A FamilySearch image of an 1851 census is, in source terms: original register (TNA RG 11/...) → microfilm → digital scan on FamilySearch. The citation lists all three.
  • Use the QuickCheck Models. Mills provides fill-in-the-blank templates for ~170 source types. Find the type, fill in the fields, you have a citation that experts will accept without quibble.

Worked examples

Census record (U.S.) — first full citation:

1850 U.S. census, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania,
population schedule, Pittsburgh Ward 5, p. 247B (stamped),
dwelling 1843, family 2104, John Walker household;
digital image, Ancestry.com
(https://www.ancestry.com/discoveryui-content/view/12345678)
accessed 7 May 2026; citing NARA microfilm M432, roll 745.

Vital record (state archive) — first full citation:

Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 67432 (1924),
Elizabeth Walker; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg.

FamilySearch image of an original register — first full citation:

St Mary's parish (Preston, Lancashire, England),
"Marriages 1849," entry no. 213, John Walker and Mary Ellis,
14 June 1849; digital image, FamilySearch
(https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33S7-9RCX-9XYZ)
accessed 7 May 2026; citing Lancashire Archives, DDX 194/3/14.

First citation vs subsequent citation

The first time a source appears in your work, give it the full citation. Every subsequent reference uses an abbreviated form — usually the source's short title plus the specific entry. Mills calls these first reference notes and subsequent reference notes:

-- First reference (full):
1851 census of England and Wales, Lancashire,
Preston, ED 7, p. 14, household of John Walker;
digital image, FamilySearch
(https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:XXXX)
accessed 7 May 2026; citing TNA RG 11/4012.

-- Subsequent reference (short):
1851 census, Preston ED 7, p. 14, Walker household.

The short form is unambiguous only because the long form was given earlier. If your subsequent reference cannot be unambiguously matched back to a first reference, expand it.

The cost of skipping this

Inadequate citation is the most common failure of GPS element 2 — and it is contagious. A tree built on "FamilySearch said so" produces children that say "my mother's tree said so," which produce trees that nobody can verify or rebuild when the underlying database changes. Citation discipline is what makes genealogy cumulative across generations of researchers, rather than reset every time a website is rebuilt.

storyBeats.text: Theodora pulls a thick blue-grey volume from the shelf behind her. The spine reads Evidence Explained — Mills. She places it on the desk between you with the same care a librarian uses for a first edition.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Eight hundred pages on how to write a footnote. You will think it is excessive. It is not. Every page in here exists because someone, somewhere, lost a piece of evidence and the next researcher could not get it back.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: An academic citation has one job: tell another scholar which book to find. A genealogical citation has five. The source. The repository that holds the original. The intermediary you actually used — film, scan, transcript. The access path — shelfmark or URL. And the date you read it. Skip a layer and the citation may be unreproducible the moment a database is reorganised.

storyBeats.speaker: A FamilySearch image of an 1849 marriage
storyBeats.text:
St Mary's parish (Preston, Lancashire, England),
"Marriages 1849," entry no. 213, John Walker and Mary Ellis,
14 June 1849; digital image, FamilySearch
(https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:33S7-9RCX-9XYZ)
accessed 7 May 2026; citing Lancashire Archives, DDX 194/3/14.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Notice three things. The register is named with parish, county, country. The specific entry is identified — register, year, entry number, names. The intermediary — the FamilySearch scan — is named with its URL and the date I retrieved it. And finally, the original repository — the Lancashire Archives, with their shelfmark — is given so a future researcher who finds my URL dead can still walk into the archive and pull the same register.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: First time a source appears, give it the full citation. Every time after that, a short form — "1851 census, Preston ED 7, p. 14, Walker household" — is enough. Provided the short form unambiguously points back at the full one. If it does not, expand it. Better a slightly long footnote than an unreachable one.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Study prompt

Take one record you have already used in your research. Without looking at any existing citation, write its full first-reference citation from scratch. Then check it against Mills' QuickCheck Model for that record type (census, vital record, parish register, will, land record, military pension, etc.).

  • Did you name the source itself with enough specificity to find the exact entry?
  • Did you name the repository?
  • If you used a digital intermediary, did you name it AND give an access date?
  • Could a stranger five years from now find the same record from your citation alone, even if the URL has died?

The answer to the last question is the only one that matters. Everything else is in service of it.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has written academic citations all their life why a single line — "Ancestry.com, accessed 2026" — is inadequate as a genealogical citation, and what the missing layers are.

questions.questionHtml: Who is the author of Evidence Explained, the standard reference for genealogical citation?
options: Elizabeth Shown Mills
The Board for Certification of Genealogists (institutional)
Donald Lines Jacobus
Val D. Greenwood
questions.correctAnswer: Elizabeth Shown Mills
questions.explanationHtml: Elizabeth Shown Mills, a Certified Genealogist and Fellow of the American Society of Genealogists, wrote and continues to revise Evidence Explained: Citing History Sources from Artifacts to Cyberspace. The other authors named are real and important — Greenwood and Jacobus especially — but the citation manual is Mills'.

questions.questionHtml: Why does a genealogical citation usually include an access date?
options: Because online databases reorganise, URLs change, transcriptions are corrected, and an access date pins the citation to the exact version of the source you actually saw
Because professional bodies require a daily timestamp on every research entry
Because copyright law on online genealogical databases requires it
Because the date proves the researcher was actually working that day for billing purposes
questions.correctAnswer: Because online databases reorganise, URLs change, transcriptions are corrected, and an access date pins the citation to the exact version of the source you actually saw
questions.explanationHtml: Online sources are not stable. A FamilySearch URL may resolve to a different image, a different transcription, or no image at all in five years. The access date tells a future researcher which version of the database you used — which lets them reason about whether your citation is still recoverable.

questions.questionHtml: You read an 1851 English census image on FamilySearch. The image is a digitised microfilm of the original register held at The National Archives (TNA) in Kew. Which of these is the most defensible first-reference citation?
options: 1851 census of England and Wales, Lancashire, Preston, ED 7, p. 14, John Walker household; digital image, FamilySearch (URL) accessed 7 May 2026; citing TNA RG 11/4012.
FamilySearch, John Walker, Preston 1851.
TNA RG 11/4012 — accessed online.
1851 census, England, Walker family.
questions.correctAnswer: 1851 census of England and Wales, Lancashire, Preston, ED 7, p. 14, John Walker household; digital image, FamilySearch (URL) accessed 7 May 2026; citing TNA RG 11/4012.
questions.explanationHtml: Only the first option names the specific source (parish, ED, page, household), the intermediary (FamilySearch, with URL and access date), and the underlying repository (TNA, with shelfmark). The other three each drop layers that would prevent another researcher from recovering the exact image — they are the most common kind of inadequate citation in amateur trees.

questions.questionHtml: You have already given the full first-reference citation for the 1851 Preston census, John Walker household, earlier in your report. You now need to refer to it again on page 7. Which is the appropriate subsequent reference?
options: 1851 census, Preston ED 7, p. 14, Walker household.
1851 census of England and Wales, Lancashire, Preston, ED 7, p. 14, John Walker household; digital image, FamilySearch (URL) accessed 7 May 2026; citing TNA RG 11/4012.
Same as before.
FamilySearch, accessed 2026.
questions.correctAnswer: 1851 census, Preston ED 7, p. 14, Walker household.
questions.explanationHtml: A subsequent reference is the abbreviated form of the first citation — short enough to be readable, specific enough to be unambiguous against the earlier full form. "Same as before" is too vague (which earlier citation? the 1851 or the 1841?), and the third option just uses the database name with no specifics. Repeating the full citation every time is not wrong, but it is wasteful — Mills' framework explicitly endorses short subsequent references.

subChunks.title: Reasonably Exhaustive Search
subChunks.hookHtml: "Reasonably exhaustive" does not mean "every record on earth." It means: every record set a competent researcher would consult for this question, in this place, at this time. Knowing what those record sets are is most of the skill.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Element 1, again — but in practice

The first element of the GPS is the one that protects you from being wrong. A conclusion supported by every record you happened to find is fragile; a conclusion that has survived every record you looked for — including the ones that came up empty — is robust. The phrase "reasonably exhaustive" is doing two pieces of work: exhaustive sets the ambition; reasonably sets the limit.

Locality-driven research

Every place at every period has a different set of records. The right first move when you take on a new ancestor is not to search a database — it is to ask: what records were created for this place in this period, and where are they now?

  • England 1538–1837: parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the spine. Bishop's transcripts are a partial duplicate.
  • England 1837 onwards: civil registration of births, marriages, deaths through the General Register Office. Decennial census from 1841.
  • U.S. colonial period: town and county records vary state by state — New England has town records; the South has county records; the mid-Atlantic varies.
  • U.S. 1790 onwards: federal census every ten years (with the 1890 loss). State censuses vary.
  • Catholic Ireland pre-civil-registration: parish registers held at the National Library of Ireland and partly online. The 1901 and 1911 censuses survive in full; earlier censuses are largely lost.

The point is not to memorise every locality's record set in advance. The point is to learn the habit: before you search, find a locality guide. The FamilySearch Wiki, the major reference works (e.g. The Source: A Guidebook to American Genealogy; Ancestral Trails for the British Isles), and BCG-published case studies give locality-specific record inventories. Start there.

The FAN principle (cluster genealogy)

Coined and championed by Elizabeth Shown Mills: FAN stands for Friends, Associates, and Neighbours. The idea: when records about your direct ancestor are thin or ambiguous, records about the people around them often resolve the question.

  • Witnesses on a marriage record are usually relatives or close friends — and may appear in your ancestor's other documents.
  • Bondsmen, sureties, and executors named on wills are almost always inside the family or close to it.
  • Neighbours on a census page often migrated together; a same-name match in a new county is much more credible if the same neighbours appear there too.
  • Godparents on Catholic baptisms, sponsors on confirmations, and witnesses on naturalisation papers all carry the same signal.

FAN research turns one ambiguous ancestor into a cluster of people whose records cross-reference each other. A John Walker by himself is one of fifty in the parish; a John Walker who appears alongside the same six surnames on a marriage register, a baptism register, and a will witness list is identifiable.

Negative searches — and why you record them

The single most common failure of GPS element 1 is forgetting to record what was searched and came up empty. A negative search — "I checked the 1851 census of all Lancashire and there was no John Walker of the right age outside Preston" — is evidence. It supports the conclusion that the John Walker in Preston is the only candidate. If you don't record the negative search, you have no defence against a future critic asking "how do you know there isn't another?"

The discipline is simple. In your research log (gen-b5), every search gets an entry — even the ones that returned nothing. The entry records: the question, the source, the search terms, the result (positive, negative, or partial), the citation, and the date.

What "reasonably" means

The standard does not require you to consult records that do not exist (most pre-1837 English ancestors do not have a birth certificate), records that have been destroyed (1890 U.S. federal census, much of the Public Record Office of Ireland after 1922), records held in private collections inaccessible to researchers, or records that no competent researcher of this question would think to look at (a French notarial archive when researching an English farmer).

It does require you to consult records that do exist and are accessible — even if it takes weeks or international correspondence to do so. The line between "reasonable" and "unreasonable" is set by the research community's published expectations, not by what the researcher feels like doing.

When to stop

You have stopped reasonably when:

  • You have consulted every record set a published locality guide names for the time and place.
  • The FAN cluster has been worked — you have searched for the same names in records about the people around your ancestor.
  • Each new search is producing only duplicates of what you already have, not new evidence.
  • You can list the records you did not consult and say why they are inappropriate or inaccessible to this question.

If any of those is not yet true, you have not yet stopped reasonably.

storyBeats.text: Theodora unrolls a parish map of Lancashire across the desk, weighting the corners with brass paperweights.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Apprentices ask me, "Have I searched enough?" The answer is never yes. The answer is, have you searched everything a competent researcher would think to search for this question, in this place, at this time? The question is locality-driven. The answer is published in the locality guides.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And when records about your ancestor are thin — and they nearly always are — you widen the lens. Friends, Associates, Neighbours. Mills' FAN principle. Witnesses, godparents, bondsmen, the families who lived three doors down on the census. The records of the cluster around your ancestor will identify them when records about your ancestor alone cannot.

storyBeats.speaker: A FAN cluster doing the work
storyBeats.text:
Direct evidence on John Walker:
  - 1849 marriage to Mary Ellis, witnesses: Thomas Walker, Sarah Ellis
  - 1851 census, Preston, household includes wife Mary, no children yet

FAN evidence:
  - 1841 census, Preston: John Walker (age 14) in household of
    Thomas Walker, labourer (probable elder brother)
  - 1855 baptism, Preston St Mary's: Sarah, daughter of John & Mary Walker;
    sponsors include Sarah Ellis (probable sister-in-law)
  - 1857 will of Thomas Walker (Preston): names John Walker as brother

The cluster — Thomas, Sarah — appears in three independent records and locks the identity.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: And the searches that came up empty? You write those down too. "Searched 1851 census of all Lancashire for John Walker, age 24–28, born Preston: only one match, in Preston itself." That negative search is evidence — it supports the conclusion that there is no other candidate. If you don't record it, you cannot defend against a critic who later asks how do you know?

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: When have you done enough? When new searches return only duplicates of evidence you already have, when the FAN cluster has been worked, and when you can list the records you did not search and say why they are inappropriate or inaccessible. Until then, keep going.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Study prompt

Pick one ancestor you are researching. Open the FamilySearch Wiki for their locality and time period (e.g. "Lancashire Genealogy 1800–1850"). Write down:

  1. The full list of record types the wiki names for that locality and period.
  2. For each, mark: searched / not yet searched / inaccessible.
  3. For each "not yet searched," write one sentence on whether it is reasonable to search next, or whether it is inappropriate to this question.
  4. Identify three people in the FAN cluster around your ancestor (witnesses, neighbours, sponsors, executors, bondsmen). For each, list the record(s) where they appear alongside your ancestor.

The list under (2) — and how many items are still in "not yet searched" — is the honest answer to whether you have met element 1 of the GPS.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the FAN principle to a beginning researcher and give one realistic example of how a witness on a marriage record could identify an ancestor when their direct records are ambiguous.

questions.questionHtml: What does FAN stand for in cluster genealogy?
options: Friends, Associates, Neighbours
Family, Ancestors, Nation
Findings, Analyses, Notes
Foreign, American, Native
questions.correctAnswer: Friends, Associates, Neighbours
questions.explanationHtml: The principle was named and popularised by Elizabeth Shown Mills. The idea: when direct records about an ancestor are thin or ambiguous, records about the people around them — witnesses, godparents, neighbours on a census, executors of a will — often resolve the identity.

questions.questionHtml: Why is recording a negative search ("I looked here, found nothing") a key part of meeting GPS element 1?
options: Because the absence of evidence in a place a competent researcher would search supports the conclusion that no other candidate exists, and the record of the negative search is the defence against future critics asking "how do you know?"
Because BCG-Certified researchers are paid by the search and need to log unsuccessful ones for billing
Because negative searches are required to claim a tax deduction on genealogical research
Because the FamilySearch terms of service require it
questions.correctAnswer: Because the absence of evidence in a place a competent researcher would search supports the conclusion that no other candidate exists, and the record of the negative search is the defence against future critics asking "how do you know?"
questions.explanationHtml: A negative search is evidence in the same way a positive search is. "I checked the 1851 census of all Lancashire and there is no other John Walker of the right age" supports the identification of the Preston John Walker. Without the recorded negative search, the conclusion has nothing protecting it from "but what if there were another?".

questions.questionHtml: You are researching an Irish-Catholic ancestor born in County Cork around 1820. The 1821 Irish census has been destroyed; the parish registers begin in 1812. A competent researcher would consider it reasonable to search which of these?
options: The Cork parish registers (1812 onwards) — they are the appropriate primary source
The 1820 U.S. federal census — your ancestor lived in Ireland
Notarial records of seventeenth-century France — the wrong country and century
The 1900 U.S. federal census only — your ancestor was born in 1820, not 1900
questions.correctAnswer: The Cork parish registers (1812 onwards) — they are the appropriate primary source
questions.explanationHtml: "Reasonably exhaustive" is locality-driven. For a Catholic Cork ancestor born around 1820, the parish registers are the appropriate primary record. The destroyed 1821 census is unavailable; foreign censuses are inappropriate; later censuses might be relevant for emigration questions but cannot answer the birth question. Locality + period determines the appropriate record set.

questions.questionHtml: Two researchers report on a difficult identity question. Whose work better satisfies GPS element 1?
options: Researcher A consulted the parish register, the census, the will of a likely brother (FAN), and the 1841 census of every adjacent parish; she also recorded the four record sets she could not access (private, archive closed, destroyed in fire) and explained why
Researcher B searched twelve different online databases — all of which index the same parish register and census — and reported a thorough search
Researcher C consulted three records that all agreed and stopped, calling it solved
Researcher D reviewed only DNA matches and concluded the question was answered
questions.correctAnswer: Researcher A consulted the parish register, the census, the will of a likely brother (FAN), and the 1841 census of every adjacent parish; she also recorded the four record sets she could not access (private, archive closed, destroyed in fire) and explained why
questions.explanationHtml: A's work is exhaustive (different record types, FAN-aware, neighbouring parishes), reasonable (the unsearched records are unsearchable, and she said why), and recorded (the negatives are written down). B has volume but not breadth — twelve databases pointing at the same two underlying records is one search, not twelve. C and D both stop short of the discipline's expectations.

subChunks.title: Conflict Analysis & Resolution
subChunks.hookHtml: Three records will tell you three different ages for the same person. That is not a problem with the records — it is the normal condition of genealogical evidence. The skill is not finding sources that agree; it is reasoning carefully about why they don't.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Conflicts are the rule, not the exception

If you trace any ancestor through more than two records, you will hit contradictions. Ages drift. Names are spelled differently. Places of birth disagree. The 1851 census says the wife was born in Preston; the 1861 census says she was born in Wigan. The marriage register says she was 22; her death certificate, 39 years later, implies she was born five years earlier than the marriage register suggested. None of this is unusual. All of it requires resolution.

Direct vs indirect evidence

Element 3 of the GPS — analysis and correlation — depends on classifying each piece of evidence on at least three axes. The most important is the direct vs indirect distinction (introduced in gen-a5; deepened here):

  • Direct evidence states the answer to your research question explicitly. "John Walker, born 14 March 1825, Preston." If your question is John's birth date, this is direct.
  • Indirect evidence requires you to combine two or more facts to reach the answer. The 1851 census says John was 26 and resident in Preston; that implies birth around 1825 and a connection to Preston, but neither is stated. To answer "when and where was John born?" you have to combine the age with the assumption that the household head was honest with the enumerator.
  • Negative evidence — the absence of an expected record — can also support a conclusion. If John appears in every census from 1841 to 1881 and then disappears, his absence from 1891 plus the appearance of his widow as "Mary Walker, widow" supports a death between 1881 and 1891.

Other axes — original vs derivative; primary vs secondary

AxisBetterWeaker
Source formatOriginal — the actual register, document, gravestoneDerivative — a transcription, abstract, index entry, or compiled tree
InformationPrimary — recorded by an eyewitness near the event (a midwife at a birth, the priest at the wedding)Secondary — recorded long after the event by someone who was not there (a child reporting a parent's birth date on the parent's death certificate)
Evidence typeDirectIndirect / negative

None of these axes are a strict ranking. A primary-information original — a parish register written by the priest the morning after the wedding — is strong but not infallible (priests miscounted ages too). A derivative source — a careful transcription — may be the only thing that survived a fire. The axes give you vocabulary for an argument, not a verdict.

Worked example — a birth date

Question: When was Mary Ellis (later Mary Walker) born?

SourceDate impliedOriginal/DerivativePrimary/SecondaryDirect/Indirect
1849 marriage register, Preston St Mary's: "Mary Ellis, age 22"~1827OriginalPrimary (about the marriage; secondary about her birth — she or the priest reported the age)Indirect (age, not birth date)
1851 census, Preston: Mary Walker, age 24, born Preston~1827Original (the enumerator's schedule)Secondary (Mary or her husband told the enumerator the age)Indirect
1888 death certificate, Preston: Mary Walker, age 66~1822OriginalSecondary (the informant — usually a child or husband — reported the age, which is famously unreliable)Indirect

Three records, two date estimates: ~1827 (twice) and ~1822 (once). The 1888 death certificate is the outlier. Resolution:

  • The 1849 and 1851 sources are within two years of each other and were recorded close to events Mary was alive for. Her stated age can be expected to be roughly accurate.
  • The 1888 death certificate's age comes from an informant — almost always a relative reporting in the moments after a death, when memory is least careful and the informant may not have known her exact age.
  • The weight of evidence — two near-event records agreeing, one far-event record disagreeing — supports a birth circa 1827.
  • This conclusion is recorded in the proof argument with the conflict explicitly named: "The 1888 death certificate's age (66, implying birth c.1822) conflicts with the 1849 marriage register and 1851 census (both implying c.1827). The marriage and census records were created closer to events Mary was alive to verify, and death-certificate ages are documented by genealogists to be the least reliable type of age statement. The weight of evidence supports a birth circa 1827."

That paragraph is element 4 in action. The conflict is not buried; it is named, weighed, and resolved on the page.

What conflict resolution is not

It is not picking the source you like. It is not averaging the disagreeing values. It is not assuming the original is right and the derivative wrong (often it is — but not always). It is reasoning from the analysis axes, weighing the source's reliability for the specific question, and writing your reasoning into the conclusion so another researcher can see — and challenge — your logic.

storyBeats.text: Theodora produces three sheets and lays them in front of you side by side: a marriage register entry, a census transcription, and a death certificate.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Three records. Mary Ellis. Born circa 1827 according to two of them; circa 1822 according to the third. An apprentice asks me which one is right. The question itself is wrong. The right question is: which one is more reliable for this specific fact?

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Three axes. Original versus derivative — am I reading the actual register, or a transcription? Primary versus secondary information — was the person who reported this fact present at the event, or are they recalling it years later? Direct versus indirect evidence — does the source state the answer to my question, or do I have to infer it?

storyBeats.speaker: Mary Ellis's birth date — the conflict
storyBeats.text:
1849 marriage register: "Mary Ellis, age 22"   →  c.1827
1851 census:           Mary Walker, age 24      →  c.1827
1888 death certificate: Mary Walker, age 66      →  c.1822

Resolution: the 1849 and 1851 records are close to events
Mary herself could verify (her marriage, her household);
the 1888 informant — almost certainly a child or her husband
in the immediate aftermath of her death — was reporting an age
they could only loosely recall. Death-certificate ages are
documented as the least reliable category. Weight of evidence: c.1827.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: I do not pick the one I like. I do not average them. I weigh each source against the specific question, and I write down my reasoning. "The death certificate conflicts with the earlier records; the death certificate is the least reliable type of age statement; the weight of evidence supports a birth circa 1827." Another genealogist who disagrees with my conclusion can attack that paragraph directly. Without it, they have nothing to argue with — and neither do I.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Conflicts are the rule, not the exception. Three records, three answers — that is the normal condition of genealogical evidence. Element 4 of the GPS is what turns disagreement from a problem into the most informative part of the argument.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Study prompt

Find one ancestor in your tree for whom you have at least three records that touch on the same fact (birth date, place of birth, mother's maiden name, occupation, anything). For each record, classify it on three axes:

  • Original or derivative?
  • Primary or secondary information for this specific fact?
  • Direct or indirect evidence for this specific question?

If they all agree, you are done — but make sure they are independent (a transcription and the original are not independent). If they disagree, write a paragraph that names the conflict explicitly, weighs the sources, and gives your conclusion. The paragraph itself is element 4 of the GPS.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a beginner why a death certificate is often the least reliable source for the deceased's birth date, and how you would weigh it against an earlier marriage register that gives a different age.

questions.questionHtml: What does it mean to call a piece of evidence direct?
options: It explicitly states the answer to the research question
It comes from an original document, not a transcription
It was recorded at the time of the event by an eyewitness
It comes from a database with no intermediary
questions.correctAnswer: It explicitly states the answer to the research question
questions.explanationHtml: Direct evidence states the answer outright ("John Walker, born 14 March 1825, Preston" — direct evidence of John's birth). The other answers describe original (vs derivative) format and primary (vs secondary) information — distinct axes that classify the same source on different dimensions.

questions.questionHtml: An 1851 census schedule lists "Mary Walker, age 24, born Preston, Lancashire." For the research question "when was Mary Walker born?", this entry is best classified as:
options: Original format, secondary information, indirect evidence
Derivative format, primary information, direct evidence
Original format, primary information, direct evidence
Derivative format, secondary information, negative evidence
questions.correctAnswer: Original format, secondary information, indirect evidence
questions.explanationHtml: The enumerator's schedule itself is original (it is the document the government created at the time). The information is secondary for Mary's birth — Mary or another household member reported her age years after the actual birth. And it is indirect evidence of birth date — the source gives age, not birth date, so you must compute. All three axes apply to the same source independently.

questions.questionHtml: You have three records of Mary's birth year. The 1849 marriage register implies 1827. The 1851 census implies 1827. The 1888 death certificate implies 1822. What is the most defensible resolution?
options: Birth circa 1827, with the 1888 conflict explicitly named and explained — death-certificate ages are widely documented as the least reliable type, and the two near-event records agree
Birth circa 1824 — the average of the three implied dates
Birth circa 1822 — the death certificate is the most recent record so it must be the most accurate
Birth date is unknowable; the records disagree, so no conclusion is possible
questions.correctAnswer: Birth circa 1827, with the 1888 conflict explicitly named and explained — death-certificate ages are widely documented as the least reliable type, and the two near-event records agree
questions.explanationHtml: You do not average ages — that is statistical confusion, not analysis. The 1888 informant was reporting an age in the immediate aftermath of a death; the 1849 marriage and 1851 census were created when Mary was alive to verify the age herself. Two independent near-event records agreeing carries far more weight than one far-event record. Crucially, GPS element 4 demands you name the conflict in the written conclusion — not bury it.

questions.questionHtml: Which of these is a correct statement about the original/derivative and primary/secondary axes?
options: An original document can carry secondary information, and a derivative document can carry primary information; the axes are independent
An original document always carries primary information, and a derivative always carries secondary
Primary information is always the same as direct evidence
Derivative documents are unusable in genealogical proof
questions.correctAnswer: An original document can carry secondary information, and a derivative document can carry primary information; the axes are independent
questions.explanationHtml: The axes are independent. A death certificate (original document) carries primary information for the death itself but secondary information for the birth date of the deceased — the informant was not present at the birth. A careful, contemporaneous transcription of a destroyed register can be the only available carrier of primary information. Treating the axes as a fused ranking is the most common analytical mistake apprentices make.

subChunks.title: Research Logs & Documentation
subChunks.hookHtml: The research log is the genealogist's notebook of intent and outcome. "I'll remember what I checked" is the most expensive lie in genealogy — and the discipline of recording every search, especially the ones that returned nothing, is what turns a hobbyist's tree into a defensible body of work.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What a research log is

A research log is a chronological record of what you intended to find, what you searched, and what came back. It is not your tree; it is not your proof argument. It is the audit trail that supports them. Every meaningful piece of research lives, at least temporarily, on a log entry before it earns a place in the conclusion.

The log answers four questions a critic — or your future self — will eventually ask:

  • What was I trying to find?
  • Where did I look?
  • What did I find — or not find?
  • How would another researcher reach the same source?

What a log entry contains

The minimum useful log entry has six fields:

FieldExample
Date of search2026-05-07
Research questionConfirm John Walker's marriage to Mary Ellis, Preston, ~1849
Source consultedFamilySearch, Lancashire parish marriages 1538–1973
Search terms / parametersSurname Walker, Preston, year range 1845–1855
ResultPositive: 14 June 1849, John Walker × Mary Ellis, St Mary's Preston, witnesses Thomas Walker & Sarah Ellis
CitationSt Mary's Preston, marriages 1849, entry 213 (FamilySearch URL, accessed 2026-05-07; citing Lancashire Archives DDX 194/3/14)

If the search returns nothing, the Result field still exists — it just reads "Negative: no John Walker × Mary in this parish in the year range". That negative-search entry is exactly as valuable as a positive one (gen-b3).

A sample row

| Date       | Question                                              | Source                                                                | Search                              | Result                                                                          | Citation                                                                                                                |
|------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2026-05-07 | Confirm John Walker × Mary Ellis marriage, Preston    | FamilySearch — Lancashire Parish Marriages 1538–1973                  | Walker, Preston, 1845–1855          | POS — 14 Jun 1849, St Mary's Preston, entry 213; witnesses T. Walker, S. Ellis  | St Mary's Preston, marriages 1849, entry 213 (FamilySearch ark URL, accessed 2026-05-07; citing Lancashire Archives DDX 194/3/14) |
| 2026-05-07 | Same — check for second John Walker marriage in range | FamilySearch — Lancashire Parish Marriages, all parishes              | Walker, Lancashire, 1845–1855       | NEG — only one John Walker × Mary marriage in range; one J. Walker × Anne (Wigan, 1853, age 38) excluded as wrong age | (search-log entry; no record retrieved)                                                                                  |

Tools — pick one and stay with it

  • Spreadsheet (Google Sheets, Excel) — minimal, free, portable, sortable. The most common professional choice. One row per search.
  • Dedicated software — RootsMagic, Family Tree Maker, Legacy Family Tree, MacFamilyTree all have research-log modules linked to people in your tree. Useful if you already use the same program for your tree.
  • Evidentia — software designed specifically around the GPS and Mills' analytical model. It walks you through classifying each source's information and evidence. Steeper learning curve; higher rigour.
  • Notion / Obsidian / a notebook — fine if you are disciplined; the risk is unstructured notes that grow into chaos.

The right tool is the one you will actually keep up. A boring spreadsheet you fill in every session beats a sophisticated software you stop opening.

The discipline of recording negative results

Three out of four searches return nothing. Most apprentices only log the ones that produced a record — and lose all the information the negative searches contained. A year later they cannot remember whether they have already checked the 1841 census of Wigan; they search again, find nothing again, and waste a session reproducing work they already did.

The fix is to write the entry before you search. Date, question, source, search terms — written first. After the search, fill in the result, even if it is one word: "Negative." Six months later, when you wonder whether the 1841 Wigan census has been checked, the answer is on row 47 of your log: yes, on 7 May 2026, with these search terms, and nothing came back.

Why this is the foundation of element 1

Reasonably exhaustive search (gen-b3) and the research log are the same discipline seen from two sides. Exhaustive search is the standard the profession holds you to; the log is the evidence that you actually did it. A claim that you have searched reasonably, with no log to support it, is not a claim a peer reviewer can verify. With a log, your claim is auditable — and a serious genealogical conclusion is, fundamentally, an auditable claim.

storyBeats.text: Theodora opens a grey-bound notebook to a page filled with neat columns of dates, sources, and result codes. She turns it so you can read it.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: This is mine. Twenty-three years of it. Every search, every source, every result. The negative searches are the fattest part of the book — three searches in four come back empty. If I had only logged the successful ones, I would have spent twenty years doing the same searches over and over and forgetting which ones I had already done.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: "I'll remember what I checked" is the most expensive lie in genealogy. You will not remember. I do not remember. Six months from now, when you wonder whether you ever checked the 1851 census of every adjacent parish — your only honest answer is whatever your log tells you.

storyBeats.speaker: A row in the log
storyBeats.text:
Date:     2026-05-07
Question: Confirm John Walker × Mary Ellis marriage, Preston, ~1849
Source:   FamilySearch, Lancashire Parish Marriages 1538–1973
Search:   Surname Walker, Preston, 1845–1855
Result:   POS — 14 Jun 1849, St Mary's Preston, entry 213
          Witnesses: Thomas Walker, Sarah Ellis
Citation: St Mary's Preston, marriages 1849, entry 213
          (FamilySearch ark URL, accessed 2026-05-07;
           citing Lancashire Archives DDX 194/3/14)

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Six fields. Date, question, source, search terms, result, citation. The discipline that matters most: write the first four before you search. Then the search itself takes ninety seconds, the entry is already half-done, and even a negative result — "No match" — fills in completely. Pre-writing the entry is what makes the log a habit instead of an afterthought.

storyBeats.speaker: Theodora of the Thousand Names
storyBeats.text: Tool? A spreadsheet is fine. RootsMagic and Legacy and Family Tree Maker all have log modules. Evidentia is built for the standard if you want a stricter scaffold. The right tool is the one you will keep up. The wrong tool is the elegant one you stop opening. Pick boring and reliable.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Study prompt

Open a spreadsheet. Create six columns: Date, Question, Source, Search terms, Result, Citation. Then, for the next research session you do, follow this discipline:

  1. Before you search: fill in Date, Question, Source, and Search terms.
  2. Run the search.
  3. Fill in Result — one word minimum (POS / NEG / PARTIAL) plus the specifics.
  4. Write the citation, in the format from gen-b2.
  5. If the result was negative, do not delete the row. Negative searches are evidence.

After ten sessions, you should have a log of perhaps thirty to fifty rows, three-quarters of which are negative. That is normal. That is the shape of real genealogical research, and it is the shape of an audit trail a peer reviewer can trust.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend why a research log that includes only successful searches is worse than no log at all, and describe what a single useful log entry contains.

questions.questionHtml: Which of these is not a typical field on a research-log entry?
options: The DNA centimorgan match value to a known cousin
The date of the search
The source consulted
The result (positive, negative, or partial)
questions.correctAnswer: The DNA centimorgan match value to a known cousin
questions.explanationHtml: A research log records the act of searching: date, question, source, search terms, result, citation. DNA match data lives in a separate genetic-genealogy log or chart — useful, but distinct. Don't conflate the two; mixing them turns both records into something neither rigorous nor easy to audit.

questions.questionHtml: Why should a negative search be recorded in the log?
options: Because the absence of a match in a record set you searched is itself evidence — and the log entry is the proof you searched it
Because professional ethics require recording every minute of work
Because the FamilySearch terms of service mandate it
Because negative results increase your match score on Ancestry
questions.correctAnswer: Because the absence of a match in a record set you searched is itself evidence — and the log entry is the proof you searched it
questions.explanationHtml: The negative search supports conclusions like "there is no other candidate of this name in this parish in this period." Without the log entry, you have only memory — which decays, and which a critic cannot audit. The log entry is the auditable trace that turns a memory into evidence.

questions.questionHtml: You searched the 1841 Wigan census for any John Walker aged 14–18 in March, found none, and moved on. Six months later you are about to search the same record set again because you cannot remember whether you did. Which of these is the professional failure?
options: Not recording the negative search at the time, so the work has to be repeated and the original conclusion has nothing supporting it
Searching the 1841 Wigan census at all — it is the wrong locality
Failing to find the entry — the entry must exist somewhere
Using FamilySearch instead of Ancestry
questions.correctAnswer: Not recording the negative search at the time, so the work has to be repeated and the original conclusion has nothing supporting it
questions.explanationHtml: The locality and tool choices are fine; the missing entry is fine; the failure is purely the absence of a log entry. Without the entry, the original work is invisible to your future self and to any peer reviewer. Repeating the search is wasted time; lacking the log entry is unsupported claim.

questions.questionHtml: Two researchers each have a tree of 200 ancestors. Whose work better satisfies the documentation expectations of the GPS?
options: Researcher A has a research log with 480 entries — about 350 of them negative — and citations for every conclusion in her tree
Researcher B has a beautifully designed tree on a commercial website with no log file and "sources" that read "Ancestry, accessed 2025"
Researcher C remembers everything she has searched and so does not maintain a log
Researcher D logs only the records she finds useful, which keeps her log short and readable
questions.correctAnswer: Researcher A has a research log with 480 entries — about 350 of them negative — and citations for every conclusion in her tree
questions.explanationHtml: A's log shape — most searches negative — is exactly what real genealogical research looks like. Her log + citations are auditable; another researcher can rebuild her work or attack it on its weakest point. B's "sources" are not citations (gen-b2); C is relying on memory (which decays); D is filtering out the negative searches (which are evidence). Only A meets the standard.
